source.title_on_document: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort

supplement.where: Supplementary Information, PDF pp. 11-41; SI pages 1-31.
supplement.holds: Rating prompts and scoring procedures (S1; SI A1-A3); allocation/balance and missingness tables (S4-S5, S17-S18, S26-S27); writing-quality means and standardized effects with parenthesized uncertainty by phase (S6, S7, S12, S19, S20, S28, S29, S34, S35); beta regressions for interview preference (S15, S25, S38); output-derived learning-rate measures (S10, S32); AI-versus-editor counterfactual comparison (SI D2, Fig. S8). S15 contains unexplained Study 4 arm labels. Most quality tables explicitly label uncertainty SE; S19 and S20 do not label their parentheses.

paper_design_summary: Three preregistered online experiments (Studies 2-4) randomly assigned Prolific participants to cover-letter editing practice with a custom AI rewriting tool, unassisted practice, no practice, editor feedback, Google search results, or an AI example, followed by an unassisted writing test; Studies 2 and 4 also tested a later subsample. Outcomes assess adherence to professional-writing principles, hypothetical interview preference, and improvement per unit effort, rather than creativity or diversity. Study 1 is an attitude survey; a separate ancillary record preserves the paired comparison of AI and professional-editor rewrites using Study 3 letters.

task.description: Rewrite/edit a poorly written cover letter to follow five professional-writing principles (Less is more, Make reading easy, Easy navigation, Formatting, Make responding easy). Not a creative or ideation task.

outcomes.name: Test-phase writing quality (no AI), GPT-4o rating
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Unweighted mean of five independent GPT-4o ratings on 0-10 adherence to the professional-writing principles; preregistered main outcome (PDF p. 12, SI A1, S1). ANCOVA adjusts for pretest and baseline covariates (PDF pp. 9-10). S7 includes Claude Haiku ratings, unadjusted estimates, exclusion of admitted outside-resource users, follow-up completers, and individual-principle scores. Validation used 100 letters and two trained raters; AI-human correlation r = .70 (PDF pp. 9, 12). This is adherence/clarity, not a creativity or originality score.

contrasts.reported: Means (SE): Practice w/ AI 5.01 (.161) vs Practice w/o AI 4.53 (.160); d = .38*** (SE .054). Text: d = .38, p < .001. Arm SDs not printed, only SEs.

outcomes.name: Writing-quality improvement per unit effort

eligibility.reason: Random assignment to generative-AI rewriting practice is explicit in Studies 2-4 (PDF p. 2, Fig. 3; PDF p. 5, Study 3; PDF p. 9, Procedure), so the random-assignment component is met. The analyzed-people threshold is independently confirmed by the 1,294-person follow-up subsample analyzed in Fig. 6A (PDF p. 4) and the 608-person subsample analyzed in Fig. 8A (PDF p. 7); these are figure-specific analyzed counts, not assignment totals or asserted regression Ns. Exact main-regression people counts remain null. The task is professional cover-letter editing, and the scored outcomes assess concision, readability, navigation, formatting and ease of responding (PDF p. 12, SI A1, Table S1), hypothetical interview preference (PDF p. 12, SI A2), and writing-quality improvement per unit effort (PDF pp. 18, 37, Tables S10 and S32). No creativity, originality or diversity across people is scored. Thus the creative-task/outcome requirement is not met: criterion 3 requires creativity or diversity on the output, rather than any output score. AI is removed during the tests (PDF pp. 2, 5, 9). The ancillary AI-versus-editor comparison uses the same professional-writing outcomes (PDF pp. 25-26, SI D2, Fig. S8), so it does not qualify as creativity context evidence. No unresolved source discrepancy changes these decisions.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted practice improved later unassisted cover-letter quality (Study 2: d = .38 immediately and .41 one day later; PDF pp. 3-4, Tables S7 and S12 on pp. 17 and 20), but creativity and diversity were not measured.
open_questions: Exact analyzed people counts for the main writing regressions in Studies 2-4 are unreported; obtain outcome-specific participant flow and per-arm analysis counts rather than infer them from missingness percentages.
Study 1's definitive survey analysis N is unresolved: 2,637 in the main text versus 2,472 in SI B (PDF pp. 3, 14).
Which Study 2 interview coefficients and output N belong in S15? It has See AI example labels and duplicates S38's without-controls column (PDF pp. 22, 41).
What is the Study 3 first-to-second session interval: following day (PDF pp. 5, 9) or two days (PDF p. 24)?
How do Study 4 follow-up denominators relate: 800 invited, 633 respondents, 608 plotted completers (PDF p. 7), 13.45% nonresponse in SI E1 and 72.04% attrition in S26 (PDF p. 33)?
Why do the main text and SI differ on Study 3 editor count (49 versus 44; PDF pp. 5, 25) and counterfactual interview effect (d = .75 versus paired d = .62; PDF pp. 5, 26)?

Why do Study 3 practice effect magnitudes differ slightly between prose and S19, and Study 4 immediate-test effects between prose and S29? Values are kept by source without correction (PDF pp. 5-6, 27, 36).
The feedback procedure refers to Studies 2 and 4 in Methods (PDF p. 9), but to Studies 2 and 3 in SI A3 (PDF p. 13); exact feedback coverage is not fully reconciled.

Separate forecaster samples of N = 150 for Studies 2 and 3 (PDF pp. 4-5) are not counted as writers. The S4 example-only practice score evaluates an AI example, not a participant submission.
